For a long time the severed flesh was carried over the sea; and white foam spread around the immortal flesh. Within it there grew a maiden — not born of womb or marriage-bed, but assembled from the wound of heaven and the salt of the deep.

First she drew near holy Cythera, and from there she came to sea-girt Cyprus. There she came forth, an awful and lovely goddess, and grass grew up about her beneath her shapely feet — the isles that would forever claim her as Cythera-born and Cyprogenes.

summary.text: Ovid's fifteen-book song of changed forms — from

and the ages of man through divine loves, mortal pride, and the punishments of heaven, until Caesar rises among the stars: a Roman tapestry woven from Greek myth, where nothing keeps its shape for long.

chapters.text: The poet opens with a promise to tell of bodies changed to new forms from the beginning of the world to his own day — and asks the gods to breathe upon his undertaking, for they themselves wrought the changes he must sing.

Through flood and famine, through rape and revenge, through contest and hubris, Ovid returns again and again to the same device: the body altered — laurel, spider, stone, bird, star — so that desire, pride, or pity may be fixed forever in a new shape.

The catalogue is not merely Greek antiquity retold: the poem closes with Julius Caesar's apotheosis and Augustus' reign, so that metamorphosis becomes the lens through which Rome too reads its own succession of power.

Around the Muses' very parentage the ancient authors diverge. Pausanias records a Boeotian tradition that Pierus, a Macedonian who gave his name to the mountain, came to Thespiae and established nine Muses, changing their names to the ones now used; and others held that Pierus himself had nine daughters bearing those same names, so that the figures the Greeks called children of the Muses were really sons of the daughters of Pierus. This rival reckoning stands against the older descent from

Ovid turns the doubled set of names into a contest. The nine daughters of Pierus of Pella, presuming on their number, challenge the Muses to a singing match and lose; for their pride they are transformed into magpies, condemned to chatter their stolen eloquence in the woods.

Hesiod's Works and Days turns this lineage into a precept:

story.text: In Hesiod's catalogue of woes, abhorred Strife bore painful Toil and Forgetfulness, Famine and tearful Sorrows, Fightings and Battles, Murders and Manslaughters, Quarrels, Lying Words and Disputes, Lawlessness and Ruin, and Oath who most troubles men upon earth.
stand within that brood, the personified Tales paired with
(Lies), powers begotten with no father to thread the spoken word through the afflictions that beset mortal life.
Their name marks a particular face of strife: the logos here is the tale or story, the crafted account that can persuade and mislead. Set directly beside
personify the deceptive narrative — the misleading word and false report — distinct from the bloodier Hysminai (Combats) and Phonoi (Murders) of open battle. As children of
rather than independent deities, they are the verbal seed of discord, the tale that turns one person against another.
no separate deed or myth. Like their siblings —

(Ruin) — they are a noun made into a force, listed and never narrated: the abstract powers of conflict that, in his moral cosmology, descend from Night through Strife to weave deceit and contention into the very fabric of human life.

over the boundless earth. They are thus a brood of the wounded sky: the same spilt blood that fathered the avenging Furies and the war-loving Giants also gave the world its ash-tree nymphs.
Their name binds them to the

melia, the ash — the tree whose tough wood furnished the shafts of warriors' spears. As tree-nymphs they are spirits of the ash groves, kin in kind to the Dryades and Hamadryads, but singled out by Hesiod as a collective born at the dawn of the present order rather than scattered woodland powers. He names them only as a brood, without individual names or further deeds; they remain a presence rather than a cast of characters, the green and martial inheritance of Uranus's blood standing among the Furies and the Giants.
Hesiod gives them a second, anthropogonic role in the Works and Days. There he tells how

the father made a third, bronze race of men, terrible and strong, sprung from the ash trees — a race that loved the groaning works of war and violence, whose armour, houses, and tools were all of bronze. Ancient readers understood this birth from the ash trees as descent from
, making the ash-tree nymphs the mothers of the warlike Bronze Race. The reading turns the spear-wood of their name into the lineage of a generation that perished by its own hands.
This Hesiodic anthropogony stands apart from the better-known account in which the human race is moulded from clay: Apollodorus, Ovid, and Hyginus all credit
with shaping the first men from earth and water, with no word of ash trees or of
. Hesiod alone roots a race of men in the nymphs of the ash, so that the origin of mankind is told two incompatible ways across our sources, and
bear their part only in his.

Melpomene's familiar role as the Muse of tragedy, mask in hand, belongs to a later Roman systematization that parceled out one art to each of the nine sisters. The early sources know no such division of labour: in Hesiod and the mythographers the Muses share the gift of song as one chorus, and Melpomene's tragic mask is a learned assignment laid over the older, undivided 'songstress'.

story.text: Pausanias says the first to occupy the land of Thebes were the Ectenes, whose king was Ogygus, an aboriginal — from his name comes Ogygian, an epithet of Thebes used by most poets. The Ectenes perished, he adds, by pestilence.

Local tradition placed a primeval flood in Ogyges' reign: in Boeotia the waters of lake Copais rose and drowned the valley, and Attica too remembered an Ogygian inundation in which the land went kingless until

in Hesiod, Polymnia in Apollodorus — name a single Muse.

Her name is built from the Greek for 'many' and 'hymn', and is read as 'of many hymns' or 'much singing'. In the earliest sources she has no separate office of her own: Hesiod and Pseudo-Apollodorus treat the Muses as a single chorus of song rather than dividing the arts among them. The familiar later assignment of

specifically to the sacred hymn — and, in other versions of the canon, to rhetoric, to mime, or even to agriculture — is a Roman-era systematization laid over the older undivided sisterhood, not an attribution found in the early Greek mythographers.

Around the Muses' very parentage the ancient authors diverge. Pausanias records a Boeotian tradition that Pierus, a Macedonian who gave his name to the mountain, came to Thespiae and established nine Muses, changing their names to the ones now used. The Sirens' mother is disputed. Against Apollonius, Pseudo-Apollodorus gives them not to

Terpsichore's familiar role as the Muse specifically of dance and choral song, lyre in hand, belongs to a later Roman systematization that parceled out one art to each of the nine sisters. The early sources know no such division of labour: in Hesiod and Pseudo-Apollodorus the Muses share the gift of song as one chorus. The narrowing suits her name, which already binds her to the dance, but it is a learned assignment laid over the older, undivided choir of song.

Hesiod lingers on the seductive power of the Graces as a group: from the eyes of the three, as they glanced, flowed love that unnerves the limbs, and beautiful is their glance beneath their brows. Thalia's familiar role as the Muse of comedy and of pastoral, light poetry — laughing mask and shepherd's crook in hand — belongs to a later Roman systematization that parceled out one art to each of the nine sisters. The early sources know no such division of labour: in Hesiod and the mythographers the Muses share the gift of song as one chorus, and Thalia's comic mask is a learned assignment laid over the older, undivided 'blooming one'.
